title: Geospatial Indexing and Queries
description: Use Redis geospatial commands to store locations, find nearby points, and calculate distances efficiently.

data.text: Redis includes first-class geospatial support through a set of specialized commands. You can add locations to a sorted set, query for points within a radius, and compute distances between coordinates. Under the hood, Redis converts longitude and latitude into a 52-bit geohash and stores it in a sorted set, which means geospatial queries are fast and can be combined with other sorted set operations.

GEOADD inserts one or more locations into a sorted set key. Each location is a member with an associated longitude and latitude. GEODIST calculates the distance between two locations in meters, kilometers, miles, or feet. GEORADIUS returns all members within a given radius of a center point, optionally with distance information and sorted by distance.

rows: Add locations to a geospatial index

data.text: A common use case is a store locator: given a user's coordinates, find the ten nearest stores. You store each store in a sorted set keyed by stores:locations. When the user searches, you call GEOSEARCH with their coordinates, a radius large enough to cover your service area, and a count of ten. Redis returns the store IDs sorted by distance, and you look up the store details in your main database.

data.title: Earth Curvature
data.text: Redis uses the Haversine formula by default for distance calculations, which assumes a spherical Earth. For most applications this is accurate enough. If you need higher precision over short distances, you can use the Vincenty formula manually after retrieving coordinates.

terms.definition: A compact string encoding of a geographic coordinate. Redis uses 52-bit geohashes internally.

The modern Redis command for querying members within a geographic area.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Redis geospatial indexes are built on sorted sets, so they inherit sorted set performance.
Use GEOADD to add locations, GEODIST for distances, and GEOSEARCH for radius queries.
Geospatial queries are O(log N + M), making them fast even with millions of points.
data.takeaway: Redis geospatial commands make location-based features like store locators and nearby searches straightforward to implement.
